explain.say: India has nearly a billion voters, more than any other country. Counting that many paper ballots would take ages, so India uses electronic voting machines, called EVMs. Look at the board. The voter stands at the ballot unit, a box listing the candidates and their symbols, with a blue button beside each.

explain.say: You press the blue button next to your choice. See the light? A red lamp glows beside that candidate and the machine beeps, to show your vote is recorded. Each person votes only once, because the officer unlocks the machine for each new voter.

explain.say: Now look at the VVPAT printer. For about seven seconds, a little window shows a paper slip with the candidate's name and symbol, so you can check your vote. Then the slip drops into a sealed box. Why do you think a paper check is useful?

explain.say: See the control unit? It sits with the polling officer and stores the votes. It runs on its own battery and is not connected to the internet. On counting day, officials press a result button and the totals appear on its screen, much faster than counting papers!

faq.q: How do you vote on an EVM?
faq.a: In the booth, you press the blue button next to the candidate you choose. A red light glows and the machine beeps to show your vote is recorded.
asks: What happens when I press the button on an EVM?

faq.a: Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail. A printer shows a slip with your chosen candidate's name and symbol for about seven seconds, then the slip drops into a sealed box.
asks: What is the paper slip in Indian elections?

faq.a: On counting day, officials press the result button on each control unit, which shows the total for each candidate. VVPAT slips from randomly chosen machines are also counted to check they match.
asks: How long does EVM counting take?

faq.q: Are EVMs connected to the internet?
faq.a: No. India's EVMs are standalone machines that run on their own batteries and have no internet or wireless connection.
asks: Can an EVM be hacked online?

faq.a: None Of The Above. It's a button on Indian EVMs, added in 2013, for voters who don't want to choose any candidate.

facts: India has used electronic voting machines in every constituency of its general elections since 2004.
VVPAT paper slips were used with EVMs in all Lok Sabha constituencies in the 2019 general election.
